article.title: From Soybeans to Data Centers, China Debate Hits US Midterm Campaigns
paras: Editor's note: this story was translated from the original VOA Mandarin article.

With two weeks until the November 3 midterm elections, the U.S., and China’s relationship is on the ballot in some closely contested races nationwide — from soybean exports and factory jobs to the cost of powering data centers.

Candidates for the U.S. House of Representatives and Senate are debating how to counter Beijing while addressing a question closer to home: Who is benefiting from those policies, and who is paying a price.

In North Carolina’s competitive 1st Congressional District, Democratic Representative Don Davis as recently as September called on President Donald Trump to secure what he called a “a verifiable, structured timeline" for promised Chinese purchases of U.S. soybeans. Davis faces Republican challenger Laurie Buckhout.

There have been signs of progress. Last week, Chinese state-owned buyers had ordered a combined 1.2 million to 1.5 million metric tons of U.S. soybeans. But sustained purchases and actual deliveries will be key tests of any trade commitments.

In Iowa’s Senate race, agricultural trade is also a flashpoint. During an October 7 debate, Democratic candidate Josh Turek said tariffs on trading partners, including China, were hurting agricultural export markets. Republican Ashley Hinson defended efforts to hold Beijing accountable for its trade practices, while pledging to support manufacturing and reduce fertilizer costs.
The push to compete with China in super intelligence, commonly referred to as artificial intelligence, is colliding with concerns about electricity costs and local control.
In Pennsylvania’s 8th Congressional District, Scranton Mayor Paige Cognetti, a Democrat challenging Republican incumbent Rob Bresnahan, has made data center development a campaign issue.
Cognetti’s campaign has criticized tax breaks for such centers and a lack of transparency, warning that residents could be left with higher costs.

Bresnahan has proposed legislation to protect communities that reject data center projects, limit developers’ ability to sue over those decisions, and require some federally subsidized projects to deliver tangible local benefits.

President Trump has made expanding U.S. AI infrastructure a national priority. At an October 3 rally in Ohio for Republican Senator Jon Husted, Trump defended data center development with a warning: “They’ll go to China.”

Husted’s Democratic challenger, Sherrod Brown, has criticized his Republican opponent's support for data centers and tax incentives, arguing that the facilities should pay the full cost of their electricity use.

Husted sponsored the Ratepayer Protection Act, which would require states to consider standards making data centers cover grid upgrades needed to meet their additional power demand. The House passed the measure, but it failed to advance in a Senate procedural vote in September. Democrats argued that it did not provide adequate protections.

The dispute is not simply whether to build data centers, but how to ensure the costs do not fall on households and small businesses. The issue is also featuring in Senate races in Georgia, Texas and Maine.
Tariffs present another tradeoff. Measures intended to protect U.S. producers can also raise costs for businesses that rely on imported components.

The Associated Press reported on factory layoffs that employers say have attributed to higher import costs, while also noting that tariffs are not the only cause of manufacturing job losses. The White House responded by saying a factory boom is underway.
Michigan’s Senate race highlights another distinction: opposing broad tariffs does not necessarily mean rejecting targeted trade restrictions on China.

Democratic candidate Abdul El-Sayed has criticized the Trump administration’s sweeping tariffs while leaving room for targeted measures tied to industrial policy. Republican Mike Rogers has defended some tariffs but called for an end to tariff disputes with Canada.
The debate underscores how trade policy toward China can also affect U.S. businesses and economic ties with other trading partners.
zh: 從大豆到資料中心，中國議題掀起美國中期選戰風波
編者註：本文翻譯自美國之音（VOA）的原文（中文）。
距離11月3日的中期選舉僅剩兩週，在全美部分競爭激烈的選區中，美中關係已成為選戰的關鍵議題——從大豆出口、工廠工作崗位到資料中心的電力成本，皆與此息息相關。
美國眾議院和參議院的候選人正在就如何應對北京當局展開辯論，同時也探討了一個更貼近民生的問題：這些政策究竟讓誰受益，又讓誰付出了代價。
在北卡羅來納州競爭激烈的第1國會選區，民主黨眾議員唐·戴維斯（Don Davis）最近於9月曾呼籲總統唐納德·川普，確保中國方面就承諾購買美國大豆一事，制定所謂的「可驗證且有條理的時間表」。戴維斯將面臨共和黨挑戰者勞瑞·巴克豪特（Laurie Buckhout）的挑戰。
已有進展的跡象。上週，中國國有買家共訂購了120萬至150萬公噸的美國大豆。但持續的採購與實際交貨，將是檢驗任何貿易承諾的關鍵指標。
在愛荷華州的參議院選戰中，農業貿易同樣是爭議焦點。在10月7日的一場辯論中，民主黨候選人喬許·圖雷克表示，對包括中國在內的貿易夥伴徵收關稅，正損害農業出口市場。共和黨候選人艾希莉·欣森則為要求北京方面為其貿易行為負責的舉措辯護，同時承諾將支持製造業並降低肥料成本。
在「超級智慧」（通常稱為人工智慧）領域與中國競爭的努力，正與對電費成本及地方自主權的擔憂產生衝突。
在賓夕法尼亞州第8國會選區，斯克蘭頓市長佩吉·科格內蒂（Paige Cognetti）——這位挑戰共和黨現任議員羅伯·布雷斯納漢（Rob Bresnahan）的民主黨人——已將資料中心發展列為競選議題。
科涅蒂的競選團隊批評了針對此類中心的稅務優惠措施以及缺乏透明度，並警告居民可能因此面臨更高的成本。
布雷斯納漢已提出一項法案，旨在保護拒絕資料中心計畫的社區、限制開發商針對此類決定提起訴訟的能力，並要求部分獲得聯邦補貼的計畫必須為當地帶來具體利益。
川普總統已將擴建美國人工智慧基礎設施列為國家優先事項。10月3日，川普在俄亥俄州為共和黨參議員喬恩·赫斯特德（Jon Husted）舉行的集會上，為數據中心發展辯護時發出警告：「否則它們就會流向中國。」
赫斯泰德的民主黨挑戰者謝羅德·布朗批評這位共和黨對手支持資料中心及稅務優惠，並主張這些設施應全額支付其用電成本。
赫斯泰德提出《用電戶保護法案》，該法案將要求各州制定相關標準，規定資料中心須負擔為滿足其額外電力需求而所需的電網升級費用。眾議院雖通過了該法案，但該法案於九月在參議院的程序性表決中未能獲得通過。民主黨人認為該法案未能提供充分的保障。
這場爭議不僅僅是關於是否要興建資料中心，更在於如何確保相關成本不會轉嫁給家庭和小企業。這個議題也成為喬治亞州、德克薩斯州和緬因州參議院選戰中的焦點。
關稅帶來了另一種權衡。旨在保護美國生產商的措施，也可能增加依賴進口零組件的企業的成本。
美聯社報導了工廠裁員的情況，僱主表示這歸因於進口成本上升，同時也指出關稅並非製造業失業的唯一原因。白宮對此回應稱，製造業正迎來一波繁榮期。
密西根州的參議院選戰凸顯了另一項差異：反對廣泛徵收關稅，並不一定意味著拒絕針對中國實施有針對性的貿易限制。
民主黨候選人阿卜杜勒·埃爾-賽義德批評了川普政府實施的全面關稅措施，但同時為與產業政策相關的針對性措施留有餘地。共和黨人麥克·羅傑斯則辯護了部分關稅措施，但呼籲結束與加拿大的關稅爭端。
這場辯論凸顯出，針對中國的貿易政策同樣會影響美國企業，以及美國與其他貿易夥伴的經濟關係。
